questions.question: Which part of a JWT makes sure nobody changed its contents?
questions.explanation: The server signs the header and payload with its key. Any change to them makes the signature check fail.

questions.question: Why is a JWT setup called stateless?
options: The server stores no login session, because the signed JWT carries what it needs
questions.explanation: With JWT the server keeps no session per user. It only verifies the signature and expiry on each request.

questions.question: A client calls a protected endpoint with no Authorization header. The app uses oauth2ResourceServer with jwt(). What status comes back?
questions.explanation: The resource server filter finds no JWT, so the request is unauthenticated and the answer is 401.

questions.question: The JWT is issued with roles ["ROLE_MEMBER"]. A client changes one letter in the payload and sends it back. What does the API return?
options: 302, a redirect to the login page
questions.explanation: The signature was made over the old payload, so the changed JWT fails verification and is rejected with 401.

questions.question: A developer puts the user's plain password into a JWT claim so the mobile app can show it. What is wrong?
options: The payload is only encoded, so anyone holding the JWT can read the password
Spring Security blocks claims longer than 8 characters
The signature will fail to verify
questions.explanation: A JWT is signed, not encrypted. Its payload can be decoded by anyone, so it must never hold private data.
